## Recall: Cartesian Product

## Recall: Performing the Natural Join

- Step 1: take the full Cartesian product.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Step 2: perform a selection in which we filter out tuples in which attributes with the same name have different values.
    - if there are no attributes with the same name, skip this step
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Step 3: perform a projection that keeps only one copy of each duplicated column.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
- Final result: a table with all combinations of "matching" rows from the original tables.
:::

::: {.r-stack}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/natjoin-1.png){width="75%"}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/natjoin-2.png){.fragment width="75%" fragment-index=1}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/natjoin-3.png){.fragment width="75%" fragment-index=2}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/natjoin-4.png){.fragment width="75%" fragment-index=3}
:::

## Recall: Condition Joins (aka Theta Joins)

- What it does: performs a "filtered" Cartesian product according to a specified predicate
- Syntax: R1 ⋈<sub>θ</sub> R2 , where θ is a predicate
- Fundamental-operation equivalent: cross, select using θ

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Example: R1 ⋈<sub>(d > c)</sub> R2 = ?
:::

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/thetajoin-1.png){width="80%"}
:::

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/thetajoin-2.png){.fragment width="80%" fragment-index=2}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/thetajoin-3.png){.fragment width="80%" fragment-index=3}
:::

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/unmatched-tables.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- We begin by trying natural join:

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/unmatched-join.png){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

## Outer Joins

- Outer joins allow us to include unmatched tuples in the result.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Left outer join (R1 ⟕ R2): in addition to the natural-join tuples, include an extra tuple for each tuple from R1 with no match in R2
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/outerjoin-tables.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
- Enrolled ⟕ MajorsIn:

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/outerjoin-left.png){width="55%" fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
- in the extra tuples, give the R2 attributes values of *null*
:::

## Outer Joins (cont.)

- Right outer join (R1 ⟖ R2): include an extra tuple for each tuple from R2 with no match in R1

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/rightjoin-tables.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Full outer join (R1 ⟗ R2): include an extra tuple for each tuple from *either* relation with no match in the other relation
:::

::: {.r-stack}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/rightjoin-result.png){.fragment width="55%" fragment-index=1}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/fulljoin-result.png){.fragment width="55%" fragment-index=2}
:::

## Set Difference

- What it does: selects tuples that are in one relation but not in another.
- Syntax: `R1 - R2`

::: {.fragment}
- Rules:
    - the relations must have the same number of attributes, and corresponding attributes must have the same domain
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
- the resulting relation inherits its attribute names from the first relation
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
- duplicates are eliminated, since relational algebra treats relations as sets
:::

## Set Difference (cont.)

- Example:

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/setdiff-tables.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"}

- π<sub>student_id</sub>(MajorsIn) &nbsp;&minus;&nbsp; π<sub>student_id</sub>(Enrolled)

::: {.fragment}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/setdiff-result.png){width="18%" fig-align="center"}
:::

## Set Difference (cont.)

- Example of where set difference is *required*:
    - Of the students enrolled in courses, which ones are *not* enrolled in any courses for graduate credit?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/setdiff-enrolled.png){width="55%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment}
- The following query does *not* work. Why?
    - π<sub>student_id</sub>(σ<sub>credit_status != 'graduate'</sub>(Enrolled))
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
- example: 45678900 will be included, but shouldn't be.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- This query does work:
    - π<sub>student_id</sub>(Enrolled) &minus; π<sub>student_id</sub>(σ<sub>credit_status = 'graduate'</sub>(Enrolled))
:::

## Assignment

- What it does: assigns the result of an operation to a temporary variable, or to an existing relation.
- Syntax: `relation` &larr; rel. alg. expression

::: {.fragment}
- Uses:
    - simplifying complex expressions
        - example: recall this expression

result = σ<sub>room = BigRoom.name</sub>(Course × ρ<sub>BigRoom</sub>(σ<sub>capacity > 200</sub>(Room)))
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
- simpler version using assignment:

BigRoom &larr; σ<sub>capacity > 200</sub>(Room)<br>
result &larr; σ<sub>room = BigRoom.name</sub>(Course × BigRoom)
:::

## SQL

- [S]{.underline}tructured [Q]{.underline}uery [L]{.underline}anguage
- The query language used by most RDBMSs.
- Originally developed at IBM as part of System R &ndash; one of the first RDBMSs.

## SELECT (from a single table)

- Sample query:

```sql
SELECT student_id
FROM Enrolled
WHERE credit_status = 'grad';
```

- Basic syntax:

```sql
SELECT column1, column2, …
FROM table
WHERE selection condition;
```

::: {.fragment}
- The FROM clause specifies which table you are using.
- The WHERE clause specifies which rows should be included in the result.
- The SELECT clause specifies which columns should be included.
:::

::: {.aside}
*Non-numeric column values are surrounded by single quotes. Table/column names and SQL keywords are not.*
:::

## How could we get all info about movies released in 2010?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/movie-table.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
A\. &nbsp;`SELECT all FROM Movie WHERE year = 2010;`

B\. &nbsp;`SELECT year = 2010 FROM Movie;`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
C\. &nbsp;`FROM Movie SELECT year = 2010;`

D\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE year = 2010;`
:::
::::

## How could we get all info about movies released in 2010? (answer)

- D is correct:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM Movie
WHERE year = 2010;
```

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/movie-table.png){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/movie-2010-result.png){width="60%" fig-align="center"}
:::

## SELECT and Relational Algebra

- SELECT commands implement most rel-alg operations.
- Basic syntax:

```sql
SELECT a1, a2, …
FROM R1, R2, …
WHERE selection predicate;
```

::: {.fragment}
- Relational-algebra equivalent: cross, select, project
    1. take the cartesian product `R1 × R2 × …`
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
2. perform a selection that selects tuples from the cross product that satisfy the predicate in the WHERE clause
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
3. perform a projection of attributes `a1, a2, …` from the tuples selected in step 2, *leaving duplicates alone by default*
:::

::: {.fragment}
- (These steps tell us what tuples will appear in the resulting relation, but the command may be executed differently for the sake of efficiency.)
:::

::: {.fragment}
- *Note:* the SELECT clause by itself specifies a projection! The WHERE clause specifies a selection.
:::

## Example Query

- Given these relations:
    - *Student(id, name)*
    - *Enrolled(student_id, course_name, credit_status)*
    - *MajorsIn(student_id, dept_name)*
- We want to find the major of the student John Tukey\*.

::: {.fragment}
- Here's a query that will give us the answer:

```sql
SELECT dept_name
FROM Student, MajorsIn
WHERE name = 'John Tukey'
AND id = student_id;
```
:::

::: {.aside}
*\*Curious? Read "The Future of Data Analysis" by John Tukey, 1962.*
:::

---

```sql
SELECT dept_name FROM Student, MajorsIn
WHERE name = 'John Tukey' AND id = student_id;
```

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/tukey-tables.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

## Join Conditions

- Here's the query from the previous problem:

```sql
SELECT dept_name
FROM Student, MajorsIn
WHERE name = 'John Tukey'
  AND id = student_id;
```

::: {.fragment}
- `id = student_id` is a *join condition* &ndash; a condition that is used to match up "related" tuples from the two tables.
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
- it selects the tuples in the Cartesian product that "make sense"
:::

::: {.fragment .sub}
- for N tables, you typically need N &ndash; 1 join conditions
:::

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/joincond-tables.png){width="55%" fig-align="center"}

## The LIKE Operator and Wildcards

- Use LIKE whenever we need to match a pattern.
- Form the pattern using one or more *wildcard characters*:
    - % stands for 0 or more arbitrary characters
    - _ stands for a single arbitrary character

## How could we use pattern matching to get info about movies rated PG or PG-13?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/movie-table-assume.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

A\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE rating LIKE 'PG%';` [&larr; starts with PG, followed by 0 or more arbitrary characters]{.fragment style="color:#3a5fcd;"}

B\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE rating LIKE 'PG_';` [&larr; starts with PG, followed by exactly 1 arbitrary character]{.fragment style="color:#3a5fcd;"}

C\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE rating LIKE '_G%';` [&larr; starts with an arbitrary character, then G, then 0 or more characters]{.fragment style="color:#3a5fcd;"}

## What about these patterns for finding PG and PG-13?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/movie-table-assume.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

A\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE rating LIKE '%G%';` [&larr; no. would also match G]{.fragment style="color:#c00;"}

B\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE rating LIKE 'PG';` [&larr; no. would not match PG-13]{.fragment style="color:#c00;"}

C\. &nbsp;`SELECT * FROM Movie WHERE rating = 'PG-%';` [&larr; no. need to use LIKE with patterns! won't match any rating!]{.fragment style="color:#c00;"}

## Comparisons Involving NULL

- Because NULL is a special value, any comparison involving NULL that uses the standard operators is *always* false.
- For example, all of the following will always be false:
    - `room = NULL`     `NULL != 10`
    - `room != NULL`     `NULL = NULL`

::: {.fragment}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- This is useful for cases like the following:
    - assume that we add a country column to Student
    - use NULL for students whose country is unknown
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/null-country-table.png){width="100%"}
:::
::::
:::

::: {.fragment}
- to get all students from a foreign country:

```sql
SELECT name FROM Student
WHERE country != 'USA';   -- won't include NULLs
```
:::

## Comparisons Involving NULL (cont.)

- To test for the presence or absence of a NULL value, use special operators: `IS NULL`   `IS NOT NULL`
- Example: find students whose country is unknown

```sql
SELECT name FROM Student WHERE country IS NULL;
```

## Removing Duplicates

- By default, a SELECT command *may* produce duplicates.
- To eliminate them, add the DISTINCT keyword:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2, …
```

## The COUNT Function

- In what follows, we'll use the COUNT function.
- COUNT is an *aggregate* function. It counts the number of values of an attribute or the number of tuples in a relation.
- We will cover aggregate functions in the next lecture.

## COUNT(*)   vs.  COUNT(attribute)

- SELECT COUNT(\*) counts the number of tuples in a result.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- example: find the total number of courses

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM Course;
```

[result: `COUNT(*) = 6`]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/count-course-table.png){width="100%"}
:::
::::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
- SELECT COUNT(attribute) counts the number of *non-NULL* values of that attribute in a result.
- example: find the number of courses that meet in a room

```sql
SELECT COUNT(room_id)
FROM Course;
```

[result: `COUNT(room_id) = 5`]{.fragment fragment-index=4}
:::

## How could we determine how many people have won Best Actor?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/bestactor-table.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

A\. &nbsp;`SELECT COUNT(person_id) FROM Oscar WHERE type = 'BEST-ACTOR';` [&larr; double counts repeat winners]{.fragment style="color:#c00;"}

B\. &nbsp;`SELECT TOTAL(person_id) FROM Oscar WHERE type = 'BEST-ACTOR';` [&larr; invalid aggregate function]{.fragment style="color:#c00;"}

C\. &nbsp;`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Oscar WHERE type = 'BEST-ACTOR';` [&larr; double counts repeat winners]{.fragment style="color:#c00;"}

D\. &nbsp;two or more of the queries above would work

E\. &nbsp;none of the queries above would work

## Removing Duplicates

- By default, a SELECT command *may* produce duplicates.
- To eliminate them, add the DISTINCT keyword:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2, …
```

## What would work?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/bestactor-table.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT person_id)
FROM Oscar
WHERE type = 'BEST-ACTOR';
```

## What about this?

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/bestactor-table.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT *)
FROM Oscar
WHERE type = 'BEST-ACTOR';
```

::: {.fragment}
[doesn't work!]{style="color:#c00; font-weight:bold;"}
:::

## Applying an Aggregate Function to Subgroups

- A GROUP BY clause allows us to:
    - group together tuples that have a common value
    - apply an aggregate function to the tuples in each subgroup
- Example: find the enrollment of each course:

```sql
SELECT course_name, COUNT(*)
FROM Enrolled
GROUP BY course_name;
```

::: {.fragment}
- When you group by an attribute, you [can]{.underline} include it in the SELECT clause alongside an aggregate function.
:::

## How many rows would this query produce?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*)
FROM MajorsIn
GROUP BY dept_name;
```

A\. &nbsp;0 &emsp; B. 1 &emsp; C. 2 &emsp; D. 4 &emsp; E. 6
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/majorsin-table.png){width="75%"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
[Answer: D &ndash; 4 rows]{style="color:#3a5fcd;"}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/groupby-result.png){width="65%" fig-align="center"}
:::

## How could we limit this to departments with only 1 student?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
A\.

```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*)
FROM MajorsIn
WHERE COUNT(*) = 1
GROUP BY dept_name;
```

B\.

```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*)
FROM MajorsIn
GROUP BY dept_name
WHERE COUNT(*) = 1;
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
C\.

```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*)
FROM MajorsIn
HAVING COUNT(*) = 1
GROUP BY dept_name;
```

D\.

```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*)
FROM MajorsIn
GROUP BY dept_name
HAVING COUNT(*) = 1;
```
:::
::::

E\. &nbsp;more than one of these works

## How could we limit this to departments with only 1 student? (answer)

- D is correct:

```sql
SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*)
FROM MajorsIn
GROUP BY dept_name
HAVING COUNT(*) = 1;
```

::: {.fragment}
- WHERE is applied *before* GROUP BY.
- HAVING is applied *after* GROUP BY.
    - used for all conditions involving aggregates
:::

::: {.fragment}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/having-result.png){width="70%" fig-align="center"}
:::

## Sorting the Results

- An ORDER BY clause sorts the tuples in the result of the query by one or more attributes.
- example:

```sql
SELECT name, capacity
FROM Room
WHERE capacity >= 500
ORDER BY capacity;
```

::: {.r-stack}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/sort-unsorted.png){width="40%"}

![](images/L03-RA-SQL/sort-asc.png){.fragment width="40%" fragment-index=1}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- ascending order by default[, use DESC to get descending]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
:::

## Sorting the Results (cont.)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```sql
SELECT name, capacity
FROM Room
WHERE capacity >= 500
ORDER BY capacity DESC;
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/sort-desc.png){width="90%"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
- attributes after the first one are used to break ties

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```sql
SELECT name, capacity
FROM Room
WHERE capacity >= 500
ORDER BY capacity DESC, name;
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/L03-RA-SQL/sort-desc-name.png){width="90%"}
:::
::::
:::
